title: The language behind ‘kangaroo’ says north and south, not left and right
body: In 1770, while James Cook’s ship was being repaired after running aground on the Great Barrier Reef, his crew wrote down words from the Guugu Yimithirr people, among them gangurru, the kangaroo. That made Guugu Yimithirr the first Australian Aboriginal language ever written down, and it has another claim to fame: instead of left, right, in front and behind, its speakers describe where things are with **north, south, east and west**, so they always know which way they are facing. Linguists debate how absolute this is, and UNESCO lists the language as vulnerable.

slides.alt: A top-down sketch of a person at a table with a plate and a cup, and a compass rose. One label reads ‘the cup is on your left’, the other ‘the cup is north of the plate’.
slides.caption: Same table, two ways to say where the cup is.

left.label: English
left.text: Left, right, in front, behind: the directions change whenever you turn around.

right.label: Guugu Yimithirr
right.text: North, south, east, west: the same words whichever way you face, so you must always know where north is.

slides.label: when Guugu Yimithirr became the first Aboriginal language to be written down
slides.text: Cook’s crew noted gangurru while their ship was repaired after striking a reef. The word became ‘kangaroo’.

slides.question: How many Guugu Yimithirr speakers did the 2021 census count?
slides.explanation: About 810, out of roughly 1,400 Guugu Yimithirr people. UNESCO lists the language as vulnerable.

slides.heading: A vulnerable language
slides.text: Only about half of the 1,400 Guugu Yimithirr people speak it; the 2021 census counted around 810 speakers, most of them at Hope Vale, about 46 km from Cooktown. UNESCO lists it as vulnerable.

slides.note: 2021 census; UNESCO lists the language as vulnerable.

slides.heading: English or Guugu Yimithirr?
